---
title: "External packages: DoubleML, EconML, tlverse"
---

This page sketches how to wire `rieszreg`'s cross-fit $\hat\alpha$ into mature DML/TMLE libraries. The recipes use the synthetic ATE data frame `df` from the [landing-page quickstart](../index.qmd#quickstart). Install the relevant external package locally and adapt the code to your data.

## DoubleML (Python)

`DoubleML` separates the estimator class (`DoubleMLPLR`, `DoubleMLIRM`, …) from the nuisance learners. `DoubleMLIRM` expects a propensity classifier in its `ml_m` slot. For ATE the Riesz representer at $A = 1$ is $\alpha(1, x) = 1/\pi(x)$, so a Riesz learner can stand in for that classifier. The wrapper below is a regular sklearn classifier. DoubleML clones it and fits it once per fold, so $\hat\alpha$ is cross-fit on the same folds as the outcome model.

```python
import doubleml as dml
import numpy as np
from sklearn.base import BaseEstimator, ClassifierMixin, clone
from sklearn.ensemble import GradientBoostingRegressor
from rieszreg import ATE
from rieszboost import RieszBooster


class RieszPropensity(ClassifierMixin, BaseEstimator):
    """Propensity classifier backed by a Riesz learner: π̂(x) = 1 / α̂(1, x)."""

    def __init__(self, learner=None):
        self.learner = learner

    def fit(self, X, d):
        # Z = (treatment, covariates); column 0 is the treatment.
        self.learner_ = clone(self.learner).fit(np.column_stack([d, X]))
        self.classes_ = np.array([0, 1])
        return self

    def predict_proba(self, X):
        alpha_1 = self.learner_.predict(np.column_stack([np.ones(len(X)), X]))
        pi_hat = np.clip(1.0 / np.maximum(alpha_1, 1e-6), 0.01, 0.99)
        return np.column_stack([1 - pi_hat, pi_hat])

    def predict(self, X):
        return (self.predict_proba(X)[:, 1] > 0.5).astype(int)


dml_data = dml.DoubleMLData(df, y_col="y", d_cols="a", x_cols=["x"])
irm = dml.DoubleMLIRM(
    dml_data,
    ml_g=GradientBoostingRegressor(n_estimators=200, max_depth=3, random_state=0),
    ml_m=RieszPropensity(RieszBooster(estimand=ATE())),
    n_folds=5,
)
irm.fit()
print(irm.summary)
```

This recipe was run with DoubleML 0.11.4 on the quickstart data (true ATE 29.5). It gave an estimate of 29.52 with SE 0.08. `irm.summary` reports the point estimate, SE, and 95% CI.

`DoubleMLIRM` clips and inverts the propensity, so this route only covers ATE-type estimands where $\hat\alpha$ is an inverse propensity. For continuous shifts, stochastic interventions, and custom estimands, use the [custom-code](custom.qmd) DML/TMLE pattern.

## DoubleML (R)

The R port has the same API, with nuisance learners from [`mlr3`](https://mlr3.mlr-org.com/). The block below is an untested sketch. It fits $\hat\alpha$ but does not finish the hand-off: you still need an `mlr3` learner that returns $\hat\pi$ from it.

```r
library(DoubleML)
library(mlr3)
library(mlr3learners)

booster <- RieszBooster$new(
  estimand = ATE(treatment = "a", covariates = "x"),
  n_estimators = 400L, learning_rate = 0.05, max_depth = 3L
)
booster$fit(df)
alpha_hat <- booster$predict(df)

dml_data <- DoubleMLData$new(df, y_col = "y", d_cols = "a", x_cols = "x")
ml_g     <- lrn("regr.ranger", num.trees = 500L)

# Wrap alpha_hat as a custom mlr3 PipeOp that returns it as predict_proba —
# see the DoubleML tutorial on injecting precomputed nuisances for the recipe.
pi_hat   <- pmin(pmax(1 / pmax(alpha_hat[df$a == 1], 1e-6), 1e-6), 1 - 1e-6)
```

## EconML

EconML's [`automatic_debiased_ml`](https://econml.azurewebsites.net/) module ships its own Riesz learner (`RieszNet`, `ForestRiesz`). The `forestriesz` package in this family wraps EconML's `BaseGRF` directly, so a forest-style fit is already EconML-native. For an estimand EconML doesn't ship (e.g. a custom continuous-shift functional defined via the `LinearForm` tracer), use `rieszreg` end-to-end with the [custom-code](custom.qmd) DML/TMLE pattern — the integration there is full transparency, not chaining.

## tlverse (R)

`tmle3` from [tlverse](https://tlverse.org/) is TMLE-native and accepts pre-fit nuisances through its `Likelihood_factor` API. You can pass cross-fit $\hat\alpha$ as a fixed treatment-mechanism factor, and `tmle3` performs the targeting step. The block below is an untested sketch of the first half of that recipe.

```r
library(tmle3)

booster <- RieszBooster$new(
  estimand = ATE(treatment = "a", covariates = "x"),
  n_estimators = 400L, learning_rate = 0.05, max_depth = 3L
)
booster$fit(df)
alpha_hat <- booster$predict(df)

# Wrap alpha_hat in a tmle3 Likelihood_factor that returns the precomputed
# values when queried, and pass it to tmle3_Spec_TMLE_ATE() in place of the
# default sl3-trained propensity learner. See the tmle3 vignette on custom
# Likelihood_factor implementations for the full recipe.
```
